title: Virtual Memory
body:
The illusion that every [[Processes|process]] has a large, private, contiguous
[[Address Space]], regardless of how much [[Main memory]] the machine actually has or how
fragmented it is. Programs use virtual addresses; hardware uses physical ones; the MMU
translates between them on every single memory access.

## What the illusion buys

- **Protection.** A process cannot name an address outside its own space, so it cannot
  corrupt another process even deliberately. This is the foundation the whole
  [[Operating System Structure]] rests on.
- **More memory than you have.** Pages not currently in use live on disk and are fetched
  when touched, so the sum of all processes' memory can exceed physical RAM.
- **Contiguity.** Your [[Stack and Heap]] look like one clean block even though the
  physical frames behind them are scattered wherever there was room.
- **Sharing.** Map one physical frame into two address spaces and you have
  [[Shared Memory]], for free, with no copying. Same trick loads one copy of a library for
  every process using it.

## How it works

Split the address space into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into equal-sized
**frames**. A page table per process maps page number to frame number, and the MMU walks it
on each access. A **page fault** is the page not being resident: the process traps into the
kernel, enters the [[Waiting state]] while the page is read off disk, and resumes.

**This is exactly the [[Cache]] argument one rung down the hierarchy.** [[Cache]] carries
the memory hierarchy table and locality of reference; do not re-derive them here. Same idea,
different pair of levels:

| | [[Cache]] | Virtual memory |
|---|---|---|
| Fast level | cache lines | frames in RAM |
| Slow level | RAM | disk |
| Miss called | cache miss | page fault |
| Miss handled by | hardware, in nanoseconds | the OS, in milliseconds |

The size of that last gap is why virtual memory is worth a [[Context Switching|context switch]]
and a cache miss is not. **Thrashing** is when it goes wrong: so little real memory per process
that every page brought in evicts one that is about to be needed, and the machine spends all
its time paging instead of computing.
